Since many of us are pushing towards getting HeapLang ready for June 8, I think it might be good to sync more regularly in this thread. This would also be helpful for me to help prioritize the PR's to help review.

Here's my current understanding on what people are doing. Please update if this is inaccurate, or you think there are other missing dependencies.

  • [x] Langauge interface
  • [x] WP
  • [x] Adequacy
  • [x] HeapLang syntax
  • [ ] HeapLang semantics (@Sergei Stepanenko in iris-lean#410)
  • [ ] HeapLang state interp (blocked on ghost map by @suhr in iris-lean#407)
  • [ ] Primitive laws (blocked on ghost map)
  • [ ] Derived lows (blocked by ghost map)
  • [ ] WP tactics (wp_pures, etc?)
    • [ ] The proofmode classes like atomicity etc.
    • [ ] IsOp by @Alvin Tang in iris-lean#401, I'm not sure if this blocks HeapLang or not
  • [ ] Examples, which ones should we target? Maybe a ticket lock?
    • [ ] Sergei's Mono Nat PR iris-lean#409. I guess this unblocks the classic concurrent add example?

I think it would be awesome to port the recent completeness result so we can try connecting Iris-Lean to Std.Do, but that might have to wait until the Iris workshop. I'm also presuming we're going to defer prophecy variables until after the workshop, unless someone else has grand designs on them.

Primitive laws is also blocked on ghost map (gen_heap required it). That's why I started with ghost map in the first place.

iris_heap_lang/metatheory.v is not blocked by anything, but it is also is not used by anything (probably including external Iris projects), so I skipped porting it.
June 8 is soon, I did not expect I would need to hurry. Feel free to fork my PR when necessary, but also tell me if you do this.

Don't worry about it! There's lots of other stuff to work on and I can take over if need be.

If you have the time, maybe you (or anyone) could stub out the ghost map lemmas? That way, other features can start being prototyped on top of it before the proofs are done.

Sure, I'll try to do it tomorrow. There are some places where I don't understand Iris notation though, like I have no idea what the following is supposed to mean

([∗ map] k ↦ v ∈ m, γ ↪◯MAP[k]{dq} v) ==∗
    own γ ([^op map] k↦v ∈ m,
      gmap_view_frag (V:=agreeR (leibnizO V)) k dq (to_agree v))
And I still have that cryptic type error with AsFractional as well.

Hi all,

I was thinking that lock spec paired with spin/ticket lock implementation is reasonable as a self-contained example. For the ticket lock we don't need any additional resources, and for the spin lock we need only tokens, which are already ported.
Regarding the design choices, I was thinking that for the sake of time optimization we could:

  • Implement semantics, ghost map, primitive laws and some parts of derived laws.
  • Make a branch, where we comment out prophecy variables part, and provide a simple state interpretation with just the heap (that is, without metainformation and without prophecy variables).
  • After the workshop, this branch could be completed and refactored to be integrated into the main branch.

This way, we can have a solid chance to have an example to show without too much crunching.

Regarding mono nat, technically, it's a part of heaplang state related to steps, but we could ignore it temporarily.
This seems like a pretty good idea to me

Cool!
I think in this case, we could relatively easily branch the efforts.
E.g., lock spec and lock implementation of choice can be done already, we seem to have all the pieces.
Semantics is mostly done (even though, it would be nice if someone with expertise in using bit ops would check if there are enough lemmas for reasoning about them).
And for the ghost map/heap/primitive laws/derived laws, we could probably start with definitions and stabs for lemma statements, create draft PRs for them without proofs (so that API is relatively established), and fill it in concurrently.

suhr said:

There are some places where I don't understand Iris notation though, like I have no idea what the following is supposed to mean

([∗ map] k ↦ v ∈ m, γ ↪◯MAP[k]{dq} v) ==∗
    own γ ([^op map] k↦v ∈ m,
      gmap_view_frag (V:=agreeR (leibnizO V)) k dq (to_agree v))

This one is like a commute law for iOwn and points-to. If you have a set of iOwn (pointsto k v) (connected by separating conjunction), then you can combine all of them into a single iOwn (set of pointsto connected by CMRA operation).
So [∗ map] k ↦ v ∈ m, ... is a syntax for folding the set of all points-to relations? Is this syntax supported by iris-lean?
Hm, maybe [^ (·∗·) map] k ↦ v ∈ m, ... would do.
...nope, it's a scoped notation.

It should be supported by BigOp notation. Take a look at this https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/blob/master/Iris%2FIris%2FBI%2FBigOp%2FBigSepMap.lean file to see some examples. I think it should work if you remove spaces between \ast and map. With the conclusion it might be more messy, as I'm not sure if general syntax ^op is supported. Here you probably will need to use bigOpM directly, passing CMRA.op to it directly, like here https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/blob/master/Iris%2FIris%2FBI%2FBigOp%2FBigOp.lean#L93.

How to apply a function to a hypothesis in iris proofmode? ihave this := iOwn_cmraValid h does not work, and I end up doing something as silly as

@[rocq_alias ghost_map_elem_valid]
theorem ghost_map_elem_valid (γ : GName) (k : K) (dq: DFrac F) (v: V) :
    ⊢@{IProp GF} (γ ↪◯MAP[k]{dq} v) -∗ ⌜✓ dq⌝ := by
  iintro h; istop
  calc
    iOwn (E := hgm.elem) γ (Frag k dq (toAgree { car := v })) ⊢
    internalCmraValid (Frag (H := H) k dq (toAgree ({ car := v } : LeibnizO V))) :=
      iOwn_cmraValid (E := hgm.elem)
    _ ⊢ ⌜✓ dq⌝ := by
      iintro h
      ipure h
      ipure_intro
      exact (frag_valid_iff.mp h).left
If you want to specialize with a Iris hypothesis you need to use $$, this is referred to as a spec-pat in tactics.md
ihave this := iOwn_cmraValid (E := hgm.elem) $$ h does not work either.
Hm. ihave H := iOwn_cmraValid $$ H normally works. Try without the implicit?

Adventures in not proving things, latest observations:

Look at this beatuful example:

@[rocq_alias ghost_map_elem_frac_ne]
theorem ghost_map_elem_frac_ne γ (k1 : K) (k2 : K) (dq1 : DFrac F) (dq2 : DFrac F) (v1 : V) (v2 : V) :
   ¬ ✓ (dq1 • dq2) →
     (γ ↪◯MAP[k1]{dq1} v1) ∗ (γ ↪◯MAP[k2]{dq2} v2) ⊢@{IProp GF} ⌜k1 ≠ k2⌝ := by
  let foo := ghost_map_elem_valid_2 (GF := GF) F K V H γ k1 dq1 dq2 v1 v2
  intro nv
  let bar : @BI.Entails (IProp GF) UPred.instBIBaseUPred
      iprop(internalCmraValid (dq1 • dq2) ∧ ⌜v1 = v2⌝) iprop(⌜k1 ≠ k2⌝) := by
    iintro h
    ipure h; ipure_intro
    grind
  have := foo.trans bar
  -- Type mismatch
  --   BI.BIBase.Entails.trans foo bar
  -- has type
  --   ((γ ↪◯MAP[k1]{dq1} v1) ∗ γ ↪◯MAP[k1]{dq2} v2) ⊢ ⌜k1 ≠ k2⌝
  -- but is expected to have type
  --   ((γ ↪◯MAP[k1]{dq1} v1) ∗ γ ↪◯MAP[k2]{dq2} v2) ⊢ ⌜k1 ≠ k2⌝
  -- exact foo.trans bar
  sorry

The biggest pain point though is the lack of any kind of rewriting (not even interactive one like conv) combined with tons of implicit arguments. But that's a well known problem.

The issue with implicit arguments, as far as I understand, is that in Rocq a lot of these implicit arguments are obtained using "canonical structures", which is a feature that Lean doesn't have (though it has been noted that it can be emulated with the unif_hint command).

I feel like to tackle this we would need to rethink a bit the definitions so they work better for Lean, but so far I believe it's more important to have a working version of Iris in Lean, over which one can later iterate to improve its UX. So we're currently prioritizing extending the things you can do with Iris Lean rather than the user experience (or this is what I think is happening, someone correct me if I'm wrong)

About the rewriting, we discussed this in #iris-lean > Bi-entailment and generalized rewriting, and while in the future we would like to have something like grw available in Iris Lean, for now if you have a bi-entailment over IProp GF you can use it with the regular rewrite tactic if you feed your bi-entailment to IProp.ext first (i.e.).

Entailment is not much a problem, the problem looks more like this:

iOwn γ (Frag k dq1 (toAgree { car := v1 }) • Frag k dq2 (toAgree { car := v2 })) ⊢
  iOwn γ (Frag k (dq1 • dq2) (toAgree { car := v1 })) ∗ ⌜v1 = v2⌝

You need to compute op under iOwn and then under Frag.
And tons of implicit stuff makes it hard to construct this by applying NonExpansive lemmas.

Yeah, in this case I found that writing the proof term using calc helped me a lot, since having the whole target written down was useful when guiding the unification. Might or might not help in your usecase though

There are some comments in the code, where I changed something, but the summary is below:

  • Most problems with implicit arguments disappear, if one stays in the Proof Mode as long as possible. That is, have H := BI.Entails.trans G J would require a lot of arguments for G and J, because the proof assistant doesn't know what PROP is used, what camera is used, and so on. If something is not supported by the Proof Mode, it is still preferable to use backward reasoning and rely on refine/apply tactics, so that proof assistant can fill the holes (e.g., ghost_map_elem_fractional and ghost_map_elem_combine). In particular, I understand why proving ghost_map_elem_combine is frustrating, since it relies a lot on rewriting. In this case, applying iOwn_mono and constructing a proof of Included and \== can help.
  • The Proof Mode can help a lot if one adopts intro patterns. In particular, when results of icases are pure/persistent/plain # allows to retain assumptions, while also getting information out of icases invocation (e.g., ghost_map_elem_frac_ne and ghost_map_elem_agree). In general, the patterns mostly follow Rocq style, but in case of errors, feel free to ask. It would help us a lot when writing documentation as well :)
  • While looking at it, I've noticed that we don't have lemmas related to interactions of iOwn and bigOp*. While it's possible to use bigOpM_weak_hom instead, probably it's better to wait for big op lemmas. Zongyuan kindly agreed to help with porting them.

suhr said:

...so in proof mode icases is used instead of ihave.

icases is the more idiomatic tactic in Iris Rocq, whose equivalent is iDestruct. In Iris Rocq, the equivalent of ihave would be iPoseProof (referencing the pose proof tactic), which I feel is less used (someone correct me on that). But icases and ihave work pretty much the same, see https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/blob/master/Iris/Iris/ProofMode/Tactics/Have.lean#L26

suhr said:

...so in proof mode icases is used instead of ihave.

ihave is also fine, it's the usual Lean have that might cause problems with implicits. In general, staying in the Proof Mode as long as possible (and using usual lean tactics only for subgoals) can help a lot with implicits.
I think in general it is: iexact > iapply > icases/ihave > pure Lean reasoning, in terms of getting the proof assistant to fill obligations.

-- TODO: Cleanup and improve interface
@[rocq_alias ghost_map_update]
theorem ghost_map_update {γ} {m : H V} (k : K) (v : V) (w : V) :
  ⊢@{IProp GF} (γ ↪●MAP m) -∗ (γ ↪◯MAP[k] v) ==∗ (γ ↪●MAP insert m k w) ∗ γ ↪◯MAP[k] w := by
  iintro auth_m frag_kv
  ihave >aux := ghost_map_delete $$ auth_m frag_kv
  ihave >⟨aux, $⟩ := ghost_map_insert _ _ _ _ w (get?_delete_eq rfl) $$ aux
  imodintro
  have X : equiv (Std.insert (delete m k) k w) (Std.insert m k w) := LawfulPartialMap.insert_delete
  istop
  refine BIBase.BiEntails.mpr ?_
  refine equiv_iff.mp ?_
  refine (iOwn_ne (E := hgm.elem) (F := (constOF (HeapView F K (Agree (LeibnizO V)) H)))).eqv ?_
  refine View.auth_ne.eqv ?_
  -- partial map equiv is OFE equiv
  intro k'
  symm
  refine eqv_of_Equiv ?_ k'
  -- equiv commutes with bind
  unfold Std.PartialMap.map
  intro mk
  rw [get?_bindAlter, get?_bindAlter]
  congr 1
  exact LawfulPartialMap.get?_insert_delete_same

wp_bind and wp_pure mostly ready for review.

I say mostly because I'd like to know your opinion on a couple of points in the implementation. The first is that I have implemented a meta-level equivalent of the fill and fillItem function to construct the simplified term in the postcondition of wp_bind. However, there's no formal link between the meta-level fill and the object level fill's implementation (which I have to later assert in the code for Qq to typecheck). An alternative to this would be to use the object-level fill and to rely on a custom invokation of simp to simplify the term.

The benefits of this approach is not needing to call simp and maybe meta-level evaluation being potentially faster than calling simp. The inconvenience is that we duplicate the implementations. I was trying to have the best of both worlds by having my fill implementation also construct a proof of correctness, but the Qq typing got a bit complicated and decided to push a version without that.

Another point is that my implementation of reshape_expr (or the equivalent function) does not consider the same number of cases as Rocq's reshape_expr. This is further explained in a comment in my PR (which I copy here for your convenience)

One discrepancy with Rocq's implementation is that my extractAllOuterEvCtx does not correspond precisely with Rocq's reshape_expr, due to how match backtracking works in the Rocq implementation. In particular, reshape_expr when invoked on #1 + #2 will consider both fill [#1 + ·] #2 and fill [· + #2] #1, whereas my implementation does not give fill [#1 + ·] #2.

I argue that this discrepancy is fine, because all ignored cases are those for which e' is a value, for which it doesn't make much sense to use wp_bind (because why would you want to have a WP over a value) nor wp_pure (because a value doesn't reduce). However, I wanted to document this here in case someone came up with a counterexample of why we would want to recover this behavior. It might even be relevant to document this in the code as well.

I'd also like to have your input on this.

As a heads up, I am currently developing a quicksort example for the workshop presentation in https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/pull/441
The idea of this example is to show how grind can be powerful for automation. Grind can actually automatically solve the sortedness sideconditions arising from quicksort, which is very cool.

During the development of this example I noticed a lot of paper cuts when using HeapLang at the moment and I am working on reducing them. The main changes I've done so far are the following:

  1. Previously, we had both Exp.val and ToVal.ofVal and it was very inconsistent when which was used and also what the notation supports. I changed this to consistently use ToVal.ofVal everywhere.
  2. It was quite verbose to insert meta-level expressions into a heaplang program. So I introduce then ?i syntax to insert the meta-level identifier into a heaplang program.

With this, we can write quicksort as follows:

def quicksort : Val := hl_val(
  rec quicksort l :=
    match l with
    | none() => l
    | some(x) =>
      (let head := fst(x);
       let tail := snd(x);
       let part := ?partition (head, tail);
       let a := quicksort (fst(part));
       let b := quicksort (snd(part));
       let e := ?cons (head, b);
       ?append (a, e))
    )

Let me know if you have any thoughts on this.

I just merged the quicksort example, thanks @Markus de Medeiros for the review! I did some more cleanup before merging, the full list is the following:

  • use &x notation for escaping terms in HeapLang, replacing {term} with &(term)
  • consistently use ToVal.ofVal (aliased to Exp.ofVal) instead of Exp.val
  • Add precedence levels to the pointsto notation such that one can omit parentheses
  • allow ∀ x : X notation for BI ∀
  • allow escaping for hl_binder
  • add hl% and hl_val% notation similar to iprop%
  • change wp lemmas to have generic postcondition
  • add a wp_rec tactic for unfolding a recursive function at the start of a proof
  • add a lemma to abstract common parts of Language.PureExec proofs
  • add wp_expr_simp and wp_finish tactics and automatically use them from wp_pure
  • clean up parsing and printing of literals
  • fix precedence levels for match in HeapLang notation
  • change notation of HeapLang binary operators to match Lean notation (e.g. &&& instead of &)

If you have some HeapLang code that is not on master, you will probably need to adapt it. See the PR changes for how to do it. (Most breaking change is that {x} got replaced by &(x).)
